title: Archimedes’ Principle
lead: A fluid pushes harder on the bottom of a submerged object than on its top, because the bottom is deeper, and the difference is an upward force on every object in every fluid. This section names that force the buoyant force, shows that it equals the weight of the fluid the object displaces, which is Archimedes’ principle, and follows the principle to its uses: whether an object floats or sinks, how much of a floating object sits below the surface, what a hydrometer reads, and how weighing an object twice, in air and under water, gives its density.
objectives: Understand why objects float or sink.
Understand the relationship between density and Archimedes’ principle.
summary_html:
• Buoyant force is the net upward force on any object in any fluid. If the buoyant force is greater than the object’s weight, the object will rise to the surface and float. If the buoyant force is less than the object’s weight, the object will sink. If the buoyant force equals the object’s weight, the object will remain suspended at that depth. The buoyant force is always present whether the object floats, sinks, or is suspended in a fluid.
  • Archimedes’ principle states that the buoyant force on an object equals the weight of the fluid it displaces.
  • Specific gravity is the ratio of the density of an object to a fluid (usually water).

figures.original_caption: (Figure 11.18) Pressure due to the weight of a fluid increases with depth since P = hρg. This pressure and associated upward force on the bottom of the cylinder are greater than the downward force on the top of the cylinder. Their difference is the buoyant force F_B. (Horizontal forces cancel.) (Figure 11.19) (a) An object submerged in a fluid experiences a buoyant force F_B. If F_B is greater than the weight of the object, the object will rise. If F_B is less than the weight of the object, the object will sink. (b) If the object is removed, it is replaced by fluid having weight w_fl. Since this weight is supported by surrounding fluid, the buoyant force must equal the weight of the fluid displaced. That is, F_B = w_fl, a statement of Archimedes’ principle.
An unloaded ship (a) floats higher in the water than a loaded ship (b).

This hydrometer is floating in a fluid of specific gravity 0.87. The glass hydrometer is filled with air and weighted with lead at the bottom. It floats highest in the densest fluids and has been calibrated and labeled so that specific gravity can be read from it directly.

(a) A coin is weighed in air. (b) The apparent weight of the coin is determined while it is completely submerged in a fluid of known density. These two measurements are used to calculate the density of the coin.

exercises.prompt: More force is required to pull the plug in a full bathtub than when it is empty. Does this contradict Archimedes’ principle? Explain your answer.

answer.solution: It does not. Archimedes’ principle says that the water exerts an upward buoyant force on the plug equal to the weight of the water the plug displaces, and that force is there in the full tub. But the plug sits in the drain, and the water presses down on its top face at a depth of the whole tub while nothing presses up on its underside except the air in the pipe. The force that must be overcome to lift the plug is the weight of the water above it, $P A = h\krho g A$, which grows with the depth of the tub, and it is far larger than the buoyant force on so small a body. The buoyant force is the difference between the upward push on the bottom and the downward push on the top; when the bottom is open to the drain there is no upward push from the water, and only the downward push remains.

exercises.prompt: Do fluids exert buoyant forces in a “weightless” environment, such as in the space shuttle? Explain your answer.

answer.solution: No. The buoyant force comes from the pressure of a fluid increasing with depth, and the pressure increases with depth only because the fluid has weight, $P = h\krho g$. In an orbiting shuttle everything inside is in free fall together, so the fluid presses no harder at the bottom of a container than at the top, the upward push on the bottom of an object equals the downward push on its top, and the net force is zero. Archimedes’ principle says the same thing: the buoyant force equals the weight of the fluid displaced, and in a weightless environment that fluid weighs nothing. A bubble in a glass of water on the shuttle does not rise, and a ball in the water neither floats nor sinks.

exercises.prompt: Will the same ship float higher in salt water than in freshwater? Explain your answer.

answer.solution: Yes. The ship floats when the weight of the water it displaces equals its own weight, and salt water is denser than fresh, about 1025 kg/m³ against 1000 kg/m³, so a smaller volume of salt water weighs as much as the ship. The fraction of the hull below the surface is $\krhoobj/\krhofl$, the ship’s average density divided by the water’s, and dividing by a larger density gives a smaller fraction. The ship therefore sits a little higher in the sea than in a river or a lake, by about two and a half percent of its draft.

exercises.prompt: Marbles dropped into a partially filled bathtub sink to the bottom. Part of their weight is supported by buoyant force, yet the downward force on the bottom of the tub increases by exactly the weight of the marbles. Explain why.

answer.solution: Follow the buoyant force to where it comes from. The water pushes up on each marble with a buoyant force equal to the weight of the water the marble displaces, so the marble presses on the bottom of the tub with only its weight less that buoyant force. But by Newton’s third law the marble pushes down on the water with the same buoyant force, and the water passes that push on to the bottom of the tub. Equivalently, the marbles displace water, so the water level rises, and the deeper water presses harder on the bottom by exactly $\Delta h\krho g A$, which is the weight of the water displaced, which is the buoyant force. Add the two: the marbles’ direct push, their weight minus the buoyant force, plus the water’s extra push, the buoyant force, comes to the weight of the marbles. Nothing is lost; the buoyant force only decides how much of that weight reaches the bottom through the marbles and how much through the water.

exercises.prompt: In a remote location near the North Pole, an iceberg floats in a lake. Next to the lake (assume it is not frozen) sits a comparably sized glacier sitting on land. If both chunks of ice should melt due to rising global temperatures (and the melted ice all goes into the lake), which ice chunk would give the greatest increase in the level of the lake water, if any?

answer.solution: The glacier raises the lake and the iceberg does not. The floating iceberg displaces a volume of lake water whose weight equals its own weight, by Archimedes’ principle. When it melts it becomes water of exactly that weight, and water of that weight occupies exactly the volume the iceberg was displacing, so the melted iceberg fills the hole it was making in the lake and the level does not change. The glacier displaces no lake water while it sits on land, so every bit of its melt is new water added to the lake, and the level rises by that volume spread over the lake’s area. This is why melting sea ice adds little to the oceans while melting land ice adds a great deal.

exercises.prompt: Why is it difficult to swim under water in the Great Salt Lake?

answer.solution: The water of the Great Salt Lake is so salty that its density is well above the density of a human body, which is close to that of fresh water. The buoyant force on a swimmer equals the weight of the water displaced, and in water that much denser than the body the buoyant force on a fully submerged swimmer is much greater than the swimmer’s weight. The net force is strongly upward, so a swimmer who tries to stay under has to push down hard and continually against it, and lets go only to bob back to the surface. Floating, on the other hand, is effortless there, with more of the body above the surface than in the sea.

exercises.prompt: The density of oil is less than that of water, yet a loaded oil tanker sits lower in the water than an empty one. Why?

answer.solution: What decides how deep a ship floats is its average density, the whole mass of the ship divided by the whole volume of its hull, and not the density of the cargo alone. An empty tanker is mostly air inside its steel hull, so its average density is very low and only a small fraction of the hull is submerged. Filling the tanks replaces that air with oil, and oil, although less dense than water, is hundreds of times denser than air, so the ship’s mass rises enormously while its hull volume does not change. The average density rises toward the water’s, the fraction submerged $\krhoobj/\krhofl$ rises with it, and the loaded ship sits lower. It still floats because oil and steel together in a hull full of oil have an average density below the water’s.

exercises.prompt:
A cube of polystyrene measuring 10 cm per side lies partially submerged in a large container of water. (a) If 90% of the polystyrene floats above the surface of the water, what is the density of the polystyrene? (Note: The density of water is 1000 kg/m3.) (b) A 0.5 kg mass is placed on the block of polystyrene. What percentage of the block now remains above water? (c) The water is poured out of the container and replaced with ethyl alcohol (density = 790 kg/m3).
  1. Will the block be able to remain partially submerged in this new fluid? Explain.
  2. Will the block be able to remain partially submerged in this new fluid with the 0.5 kg mass placed on top? Explain.
(d) Without using a container of water, explain how you could determine the density of the polystyrene mentioned above if the material instead were spherical.

parts.hint: The fraction submerged is the block’s density divided by the water’s, and one tenth of the block is under.
The block and the mass together must displace their combined weight of water; the block is 1000 cm³ and its own mass is 0.1 kg.

answer.solution: (a) 100 kg/m<sup>3</sup> (b) 60% (c) yes; yes (76% will be submerged) (d) answers vary

exercises.prompt: What fraction of ice is submerged when it floats in freshwater, given the density of water at 0°C is very close to $1000\ \text{kg/m}^3$?

answer.hint: The fraction submerged is the ice’s density divided by the water’s; Table 11.1 gives ice at 0°C as 0.917 × 10³ kg/m³.

exercises.prompt: Find the density of a fluid in which a hydrometer having a density of $0.750\ \text{g/mL}$ floats with $92.0\%$ of its volume submerged.

answer.hint: Solve the fraction submerged, $\krhoobj/\krhofl$, for the fluid’s density, and convert grams per milliliter to kilograms per cubic meter.

exercises.prompt: Bird bones have air pockets in them to reduce their weight—this also gives them an average density significantly less than that of the bones of other animals. Suppose an ornithologist weighs a bird bone in air and in water and finds its mass is $45.0\ \text{g}$ and its apparent mass when submerged is $3.60\ \text{g}$ (the bone is watertight). (a) What mass of water is displaced? (b) What is the volume of the bone? (c) What is its average density?

parts.hint: The apparent mass loss is the mass of water displaced.
Water has a density of 1.000 g/cm³, so the volume of water displaced, which is the bone’s volume, follows at once.
Divide the bone’s mass in air by its volume.

exercises.prompt: Archimedes’ principle can be used to calculate the density of a fluid as well as that of a solid. Suppose a chunk of iron with a mass of 390.0 g in air is found to have an apparent mass of 350.5 g when completely submerged in an unknown liquid. (a) What mass of fluid does the iron displace? (b) What is the volume of iron, using its density as given in Table 11.1 (c) Calculate the fluid’s density and identify it.

parts.hint: The apparent mass loss is the mass of fluid displaced.
Table 11.1 gives iron as 7.8 g/cm³; the volume is the mass in air divided by that.
The fluid displaced has the volume of the iron and the mass found in part (a); compare the density with the liquids of Table 11.1.

exercises.prompt: Some fish have a density slightly less than that of water and must exert a force (swim) to stay submerged. What force must an 85.0-kg grouper exert to stay submerged in salt water if its body density is $1015\ \text{kg/m}^3$?

answer.hint: Find the fish’s volume from its mass and density, then the buoyant force as the weight of that volume of salt water (1025 kg/m³ from Table 11.1); the force the fish must exert downward is the buoyant force less its weight.

exercises.prompt: (a) What is the density of a woman who floats in freshwater with $4.00\%$ of her volume above the surface? This could be measured by placing her in a tank with marks on the side to measure how much water she displaces when floating and when held under water (briefly). (b) What percent of her volume is above the surface when she floats in seawater?

parts.hint: The fraction submerged, 0.960, is her density divided by the water’s.
In seawater of 1025 kg/m³ the fraction submerged is her density divided by that, and what is left is above.

answer.solution: (a) $960\ \text{kg/m}^3$ (b) $6.34\%$. She indeed floats more in seawater.

exercises.prompt: A simple compass can be made by placing a small bar magnet on a cork floating in water. (a) What fraction of a plain cork will be submerged when floating in water? (b) If the cork has a mass of 10.0 g and a 20.0-g magnet is placed on it, what fraction of the cork will be submerged? (c) Will the bar magnet and cork float in ethyl alcohol?

parts.hint: Table 11.1 gives cork as 0.24 × 10³ kg/m³, and the fraction submerged is that divided by the water’s density.
The cork and the magnet together must displace 30.0 g of water; the cork’s volume follows from its mass and density.

answer.solution: (a) $0.24$ (b) $0.68$ (c) Yes, the cork will float because $\krhoobj < \krho_{\text{ethyl alcohol}}\ (0.678\ \text{g/cm}^3 < 0.79\ \text{g/cm}^3)$

exercises.prompt: Scurrilous con artists have been known to represent gold-plated tungsten ingots as pure gold and sell them at prices much below gold value but deservedly far above the cost of tungsten. With what accuracy must you be able to measure the mass of such an ingot in and out of water to tell that it is almost pure tungsten rather than pure gold?

answer.hint: The apparent mass loss is the mass of water displaced, which is the ingot’s mass divided by its density; compare that loss for gold (19.32 g/cm³) and for tungsten (19.30 g/cm³) as a fraction of the mass in air.

exercises.prompt: Referring to Figure 11.19, prove that the buoyant force on the cylinder is equal to the weight of the fluid displaced (Archimedes’ principle). You may assume that the buoyant force is $\kFtwo - \kFone$ and that the ends of the cylinder have equal areas $A$. Note that the volume of the cylinder (and that of the fluid it displaces) equals $(h_2 - h_1)A$.

answer.solution: $F_{\text{net}} = \kFtwo - \kFone = P_2 A - P_1 A = (P_2 - P_1)A = (h_2\krhofl g - h_1\krhofl g)A = (h_2 - h_1)\krhofl gA$ where $\krhofl$ = density of fluid. Therefore, $F_{\text{net}} = (h_2 - h_1)A\krhofl g = V_{\text{fl}}\krhofl g = m_{\text{fl}}g = \kwfl$ where $\kwfl$ is the weight of the fluid displaced.
